headline: In Your Words Activity — Vocabulary Production Closer for ESL Lessons
outcomes: Students leave the lesson having actively used at least one key word in a real, self-generated sentence — not just recognised it on a worksheet
Build ownership of new vocabulary: choosing which word to use gives students agency and makes the production task feel personal rather than mechanical
Final consolidation in under 5 minutes — a low-effort, high-impact closing routine that reinforces the lesson's language focus
Teacher gets a quick formative snapshot: the submitted sentences reveal who has understood the word's meaning and register
howItWorks: At the end of the lesson, the teacher launches In Your Words — the lesson's key vocabulary words appear on student devices
Each student picks one word and writes a genuine sentence using it — something true about their life, opinion, or experience
Sentences are submitted and displayed on the teacher screen for a brief class share
The teacher highlights strong examples before closing the session
teacherUseCases: Lesson closer — replace the 'write these words in your notebook' instruction with a live production task that takes the same time but produces real sentences
Formative check — see at a glance which words students reached for and whether their sentences show accurate understanding of meaning and collocations
Speaking prompt — use the submitted sentences as conversation starters: 'Ahmad wrote that he feels ambitious when he plays chess — tell us more.'

faq.q: Why 'in your words' rather than a standard definition task?
faq.a: Copying a definition proves nothing about understanding. Writing your own sentence with the word requires you to understand its meaning, its grammatical pattern, and how it fits a real context. One sentence written by the student is worth ten definitions copied from a board.

faq.q: What if a student's sentence contains errors?
faq.a: The activity captures output, not just recall — some errors are expected, especially for new vocabulary. The teacher decides which sentences to show and how much correction to offer. Use errors as teaching moments rather than marking them down.

faq.q: Can students see each other's sentences?
faq.a: Yes — once the teacher moves to the review phase, submitted sentences appear on the teacher screen. This is typically projected, so the class sees them together. Teachers can hide specific sentences before displaying if needed.

faq.q: Which words appear for students to choose from?
faq.a: The words come from the session's reference vocabulary list — either generated by the AI from the lesson topic or added manually by the teacher before the session. Students see 4–6 words and pick the one they feel most confident using.

faq.q: Is In Your Words suitable for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. Lower-level students can write simple sentences with high-frequency vocabulary. The 'choose your word' mechanic lets weaker students pick a word they know rather than being assigned the hardest item on the list.
Yes. Students access it through a shared browser link — no download or sign-in required.
